title: The Case for Letting China In
gist: Biden's former NEC director argues America is undermining its own industrial policy by shutting out foreign capital and know-how: CFIUS only weighs risk and never opportunity, licensing deals fall into an unregulated gray zone, and the frontier of knowledge in batteries, EVs and energy storage now sits in China — so the Ford-CATL Michigan licensing structure, not exclusion, is the template for catching up.

themes.theme: The self-defeating turn against foreign capital

insights.claim: American hostility to foreign investment now extends beyond China to allies, with CEA chair Stephen Miran suggesting fees on foreign holdings of U.S. assets including allied ones, and Senators Tammy Baldwin and Josh Hawley introducing bipartisan legislation to tax foreign capital inflows outright.
insights.speaker: Brian Deese
insights.so_what: A bipartisan tax on foreign capital inflows is a tail risk for U.S. asset valuations and Treasury demand that markets are not pricing.
insights.locator: Stephen Miran, the chair of the president’s Council of Economic Advisers

insights.claim: The United States is undermining its own industrial policy by denying itself the tools to become globally competitive in crucial sectors, because its investment-screening regime is overzealous.
insights.speaker: Brian Deese
insights.so_what: Frames capital-control creep as the main execution risk to the CHIPS-era reindustrialization trade.
insights.quote: The United States is undermining its own industrial policy.
insights.locator: At the federal, state, and local level

insights.claim: Washington has an elaborate apparatus for saying no to inbound investment but almost no mechanism for getting to yes, which is a structural gap rather than a discretionary policy choice.
insights.speaker: Brian Deese
insights.so_what: Explains why announced foreign investments repeatedly fail to convert into built capacity — a persistent gap between headline pledges and capex.
insights.quote: Washington has an elaborate apparatus for saying no to inbound investment but few ways of getting to yes.
insights.locator: What the country needs is a new framework

insights.claim: Restrictions are blocking American enterprises from harnessing the latest advances in data storage, critical mineral processing and chip-making at the federal, state and local levels simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Brian Deese
insights.so_what: Critical mineral processing capacity in the U.S. will lag targets because the required process knowledge is being legally excluded.
insights.locator: At the federal, state, and local level, those in power are taking steps

insights.claim: The historical American pattern is absorbing foreign know-how: French investment brought Éleuthère Irénée du Pont's advanced manufacturing expertise to found DuPont in 1802, which became the biggest purveyor of explosives to the U.S. government and stayed central to U.S. chemicals for centuries.
insights.speaker: Brian Deese
insights.so_what: Historical precedent that technology import, not autarky, has been the U.S. route to strategic industrial capability.

insights.claim: The GM-Toyota joint venture that reopened a shuttered plant in Fremont, California in the early 1980s turned a failed factory into the most productive auto assembly plant in the United States within two years while largely retaining the same American workforce, and the Toyota methods GM absorbed are now standard across U.S. auto manufacturing.
insights.speaker: Brian Deese
insights.so_what: The strongest empirical case that foreign process knowledge, not capital or labor, is the binding constraint on U.S. manufacturing productivity.
insights.locator: In the early 1980s, when U.S. car companies were lagging

insights.claim: The CHIPS and Science Act deliberately replicated that model with semiconductors, funding domestic and foreign firms alike to build fabs and train American workers, and funding the National Semiconductor Technology Center to facilitate technology transfer between domestic and foreign chipmakers operating in the United States, while barring recipients from expanding advanced chip capacity in China.
insights.speaker: Brian Deese
insights.so_what: The CHIPS design is explicitly a technology-absorption program, so its success metric is trained workers and transferred process knowledge, not fab count.
insights.locator: The CHIPS and Science Act was designed to replicate

insights.claim: China is now at the forefront of many critical technologies including electric vehicles and energy storage, and gaining access to that knowledge via foreign investment is in many cases the only way for the United States to catch up.
insights.speaker: Brian Deese
insights.so_what: The sharpest against-consensus call in the piece: U.S. battery and EV competitiveness requires Chinese licensing, so blanket exclusion locks in a permanent lag.
insights.quote: Gaining access to that knowledge via foreign investment is, in many cases, the only way for the United States to catch up.
insights.locator: China is now at the forefront of many critical technologies

insights.claim: China built its own technological base by luring foreign firms with cheap labor, low taxes and market access — in 2018 it drew Tesla to Shanghai with cheap land, low-interest state loans, tax breaks and full ownership of its plant, and Chinese automakers absorbed what they needed from Tesla to propel the domestic EV sector forward.
insights.speaker: Brian Deese
insights.so_what: The Tesla-Shanghai playbook is the explicit model being recommended to Washington in reverse — and a warning about what technology transfer costs the transferring firm.
insights.locator: Indeed, China itself followed the same playbook

insights.claim: Ford's multibillion-dollar Marshall, Michigan battery plant licenses technology and know-how from CATL while Ford fully owns the facility, with a long-term agreement to train Ford workers on CATL's core processes so Ford could eventually design and produce its own batteries without Chinese licenses.
insights.speaker: Brian Deese
insights.so_what: The structural template — licensing plus training, no foreign ownership — for any U.S. firm seeking Chinese process technology under political scrutiny.
insights.locator: In 2023, Ford announced a multibillion dollar plant

insights.claim: Oren Cass's argument that allowing Chinese companies to invest in the United States would be 'an unforced error of world-historic proportions' represents the consensus the author is explicitly rejecting.
insights.speaker: Brian Deese
insights.so_what: Marks the live intellectual battle line within U.S. industrial policy — the outcome determines whether Chinese battery and EV technology can be legally licensed.
insights.quote: an unforced error of world-historic proportions
insights.locator: The analyst Oren Cass, for instance, recently argued

insights.claim: CFIUS is backlogged and overly cautious: in 2024 applicants withdrew and refiled nearly a quarter of all notices, and total filings have declined because the lengthy process discourages companies from even trying.
insights.speaker: Brian Deese
insights.so_what: A 25 percent withdraw-and-refile rate is a hard measure of deal friction — it lengthens timelines and raises break risk on any U.S. cross-border transaction.
insights.quote: In 2024, applicants withdrew and refiled nearly a quarter of all notices.
insights.locator: The Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States

insights.claim: CFIUS can approve a deal only by certifying there are no unresolved security concerns, meaning a transaction that would benefit national security on balance still dies if doubt lingers about any single component — the committee accounts for risk but never for opportunity.
insights.speaker: Brian Deese
insights.so_what: A precise legal mechanism explaining systematic U.S. under-approval of strategic deals; changing this standard would be the single highest-leverage reform to watch.
insights.quote: In other words, CFIUS only takes risk into account, not opportunity.
insights.locator: Most important, CFIUS should change how it judges

insights.claim: Licensing arrangements fall into a regulatory gray zone with no formal review or approval process, which is why Congress spent years threatening to disqualify Ford's Michigan plant from a tax credit and investigating it for security risks.
insights.speaker: Brian Deese
insights.so_what: Absence of a safe-harbor process makes licensing deals politically fragile after capital is committed — a specific stranded-capex risk for battery and chip projects.
insights.locator: In other cases, the problem is a lack of regulation altogether

insights.claim: CFIUS's exemption list currently covers only Australia, Canada, New Zealand and the United Kingdom, and should be expanded to Japan, South Korea and European countries, with filing exemptions for low-risk deals and rapid approval for pre-vetted investors.
insights.speaker: Brian Deese
insights.so_what: Japanese and Korean acquirers currently face full screening — an expansion of the exemption list would be a direct catalyst for allied inbound M&A into the U.S.
insights.locator: When it comes to allies and partners, CFIUS should simplify

insights.claim: BAE Systems shows the workable model: wholly owned by a British parent yet employing roughly 35,000 Americans, generating close to $13.6 billion in annual sales, among the Pentagon's largest suppliers and deeply involved in classified projects, because a FOCI special agreement installs a separate U.S. board of cleared American directors and firewalls shielding technology from the parent.
insights.speaker: Brian Deese
insights.so_what: A proven governance structure that permits foreign ownership of sensitive U.S. assets — the legal precedent for unlocking blocked deals in chips, batteries and drones.

insights.claim: The Defense Department's Foreign Ownership, Control, or Influence framework should be extended beyond classified contractors to firms making advanced chips, batteries, drones or critical software, with the Department of Commerce overseeing it immediately under existing authorities including some granted by the CHIPS Act.
insights.speaker: Brian Deese
insights.so_what: Commerce is already negotiating FOCI-like arrangements with semiconductor companies — watch for this becoming the de facto approval channel for sensitive foreign deals.
insights.locator: Today, the FOCI regime applies only to companies

insights.claim: The Trump administration has treated announcements of major foreign investments as ends unto themselves while showing little appetite for building a process to encourage safe deals, meaning headline investment pledges are unlikely to convert into durable capacity.
insights.speaker: Brian Deese
insights.so_what: Discount announced foreign investment totals: without an approval process, pledged dollars and built plants will diverge.
